name: Dayak (Ngaju)
confidence_why: Hardeland's 1858 grammar and Mihing and Stokhof's 1977 phonology of the Pulau Petak dialect both place word stress on the penultimate syllable, but Kaufman and Himmelmann (2024) report the impression, offered without data, that Ngaju shows even prominence across syllables and may lack word stress altogether.
catalog_quote: Jedes Wort hat nur auf einer Sylbe den Accent. Derselbe fällt, wie die vielen oben angegebenen Beispiele zeigen, auf die vorletzte Sylbe, die ja auch in der Regel die Hauptsylbe des Stammwortes ist. Wo indess, in durch Suffixe abgeleiteten Wörtern, diese Hauptsylbe zur drittletzten Sylbe wird, bleibt der Accent doch auf der Penultima

new_statements.quote: The distribution of the stressless Java prototype has yet to be investigated systematically, as it has only recently gained acceptance as an independent type. [...] It is unclear whether many Malayic languages of Borneo and Sumatra also belong to this type. Ngaju Dayak in Central Kalimantan, impressionistically, at least, appears to show remarkably even prominence across syllables. Tadmor (2000) posits that lack of lexical accent is a general western feature that extends through Sumatra and Borneo. It seems, however, that Sumatra and Borneo show considerable variation, in addition to ongoing changes induced by contact with varieties of Malay.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog (StressTyp2 record 'StressTyp2') gives Ngaju a fixed penultimate rule (penultimate stress). Kaufman & Himmelmann instead suggest, impressionistically, that Ngaju Dayak has no word stress at all (even prominence across syllables, stressless 'Java prototype'). That is a different type (stressless vs. fixed penult), though the authors present it as an unverified impression.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The authors tentatively place Ngaju Dayak in their 'Java prototype' (languages without word-based stress): on their own auditory impression the syllables of a word show remarkably even prominence, i.e. no syllable is singled out as stressed. The statement is explicitly impressionistic and hedged ('impressionistically, at least, appears'), not based on instrumental or systematic data; the chapter as a whole argues that prominence in such languages is phrasal, not lexical.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Ngaju; the authors add that Sumatra and Borneo 'show considerable variation' and ongoing contact-induced change from Malay, so the placement in the stressless type is provisional.
new_statements.identity_note: Kaufman & Himmelmann refer to 'Ngaju Dayak in Central Kalimantan' generally, no dialect named. Ristati 2006 is on Dayak Ngaju without dialect specification in the abstract. Iper et al. 1998 (not opened) is about Katingan, a related variety along the Katingan river that the 1991 and 2013 Ngaju grammars held by the project treat as a separate neighbouring language/dialect area ('bahasa Katingan'); any stress statement from it would be about Katingan, not Ngaju proper.

new_statements.relation_note: Non-phonemic (predictable) stress is compatible with the catalog's fixed penultimate rule, and adds the detail that no suprasegmental contrast exists; it is also compatible with Kaufman & Himmelmann's stressless reading. It does not itself state a placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The abstract only states that suprasegmental features (stress, length, tone) are not phonemic in Ngaju, i.e. stress is non-contrastive. Where stress falls (if the thesis assigns a position at all) is not given in the abstract; the thesis has a dedicated suprasegmental section but the full text is not open.
new_statements.identity_note: Kaufman & Himmelmann refer to 'Ngaju Dayak in Central Kalimantan' generally, no dialect named. Ristati 2006 is on Dayak Ngaju without dialect specification in the abstract. Iper et al. 1998 (not opened) is about Katingan, a related variety along the Katingan river that the 1991 and 2013 Ngaju grammars held by the project treat as a separate neighbouring language/dialect area ('bahasa Katingan'); any stress statement from it would be about Katingan, not Ngaju proper.

readall_conflicts: The catalog's StressTyp2 record gives Ngaju fixed penultimate stress. The one substantive new source read, Kaufman & Himmelmann (2024, submitted MS p. 4), instead suggests, on explicit auditory impression only, that Ngaju Dayak shows 'remarkably even prominence across syllables' and may belong to the stressless 'Java prototype' (citing Tadmor 2000 for lack of lexical accent as a general western Indonesian feature) — a different type from the catalog's fixed penult, but hedged and unverified. Ristati (2006, abstract only) says Ngaju has no suprasegmental phonemes, which is compatible with either a predictable penultimate rule or stresslessness and settles nothing about placement. A further complication outside the assigned list: the Balai Bahasa 'Tata Bahasa Dayak Ngaju' (2013, already held by the project as, section 2.6 'Fonem suprasegmental', p. 30) claims length and stress ('tekanan') are meaning-distinguishing suprasegmental phonemes, but its 'stress' examples ([papaʔ] 'kotor' vs [papak] 'ketok', [hekaʔ] vs [hekak], etc.) are final glottal-stop vs /k/ contrasts, not stress contrasts, so that claim does not support contrastive stress and conflicts with Ristati's 'no suprasegmental phonemes'. No source opened states a penultimate placement; the penult rule rests on the catalog record alone.

audit.reasoning: Both deciding quotations are verbatim in copies we hold at the cited places (Hardeland 1858:18-19, confirmed by page marker and heading; Mihing & Stokhof 1977:55 sec. 3.3.3, confirmed by re-scanned of the scan we hold's page 7 showing folio 55). The classification rests on the language's only full reference grammar plus an independent 1977 phonology article on a named dialect, 120 years apart, agreeing on penultimate, non-contrastive stress; the database entries (StressTyp2, Gordon 2002) derive from the same 1977 article we hold. Nothing better exists in Glottolog's list: the openly available Indonesian sketches (1991, 2013, downloaded now) are silent or confused on stress, and Ristati 2006 is an unpublished MA thesis. sources.quote: "In phonemic transcription the place of stress is not indicated because it is not functional. According to our investigation the place of the stress is on the penultimate syllable except when followed by the third person singular possessive marker or/and a place/time marker. In this case stress remains on the penultimate syllable of the word base: ['anak-] 'child'; ['anakah, 'anakeh] 'his child'; ['anakahtE?, 'anakehtE?] 'that child of his'" (Mihing & Stokhof 1977:55, section 3.3.3). sources.quote: "Every word has the accent on only one syllable. It falls, as the many examples given above show, on the penultimate syllable, which as a rule is also the main syllable of the stem word. Where, however, in words derived by suffixes this main syllable becomes the antepenult, the accent nevertheless remains on the penultima, thus shifting from the originally stressed syllable onto the (formerly) unstressed syllable of the stem."
